title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
wiki_lead:
Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein ( VIT-gən-s(h)tyne; Austrian German: [ˈluːdvɪk ˈjoːsɛf ˈjoːhan ˈvɪtɡn̩ʃtaɪn]; 26 April 1889 – 29 April 1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language.
Wittgenstein was born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families. From 1911 to 1913, he studied at the University of Cambridge under Bertrand Russell and interacted closely with John Maynard Keynes and G. E. Moore, among others. During this time, he inherited a fortune, part of which he donated to various poets and artists and the rest of which he gave to his siblings. He also began what would become his first important philosophical work. However, at the start of World War I, he left academia to enlist in the Austro-Hungarian Army. After a series of personal adversities—including the death of his older brother by suicide (the third of his older brothers to die by suicide during his lifetime), the death of his close friend and perhaps lover David Pinsent, and his imprisonment in an Italian prisoner of war camp—he became depressed. He worked as a schoolteacher around Vienna. Despite these setbacks, his philosophical work was published in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus in 1921, followed by an English translation in 1922 with help from Frank P. Ramsey, to considerable discussion and acclaim.
At the encouragement of Russell, Keynes, and Ramsey, Wittgenstein returned to Cambridge, where he taught from 1930 to 1947, giving lectures on philosophy, often permeated by his original research. During World War II, he left academia again to work at the Guy's Hospital in London and at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle upon Tyne. Wittgenstein would not publish another philosophical work during his lifetime, but following his death in 1951, his voluminous manuscripts were edited and published posthumously. The first and best-known of this posthumous series is the 1953 book Philosophical Investigations.
Wittgenstein's philosophy is often divided into an early period, exemplified by the Tractatus, and a later period, articulated primarily in the Philosophical Investigations. The early Wittgenstein was concerned with the logical relationship between propositions and the world, and he believed that by providing an account of the logic underlying this relationship, he had solved all philosophical problems. The later Wittgenstein rejected many of the assumptions of the Tractatus, arguing that the meaning of words is best understood as their use within a given language game.
Wittgenstein was well regarded among academics during his lifetime, and was decorated for his courage during World War I. However, he encountered controversy during his time as a primary school teacher in rural Austria in the 1920s for his use of violent corporal punishment on girls and boys (see the Haidbauer incident). His work (both early and later) has been described as controversial and sparked a number of different reactions. Later philosophers and commentators have generally agreed that he is one of the most important figures in 20th-century philosophy.

Background


The Wittgensteins

According to a family tree prepared in Jerusalem after World War II, Wittgenstein's paternal great-great-grandfather was Moses Meier, an Ashkenazi Jewish land agent who lived with his wife, Brendel Simon, in Bad Laasphe in the Principality of Wittgenstein, Westphalia. In July 1808, Napoleon issued a decree that everyone, including Jews, must adopt an inheritable family surname, so Meier's son, also Moses, took the name of his employers, the Sayn-Wittgensteins, and became Moses Meier Wittgenstein. His son, Hermann Christian Wittgenstein — who took the middle name "Christian" to distance himself from his Jewish background — married Fanny Figdor, also Jewish, who converted to Protestantism just before they married, and the couple founded a successful business trading in wool in Leipzig. grok_lead: Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein (26 April 1889 â 29 April 1951) was an Austrian-born philosopher who became a British subject and exerted a transformative influence on 20th-century analytic philosophy, especially in logic, the philosophy of mathematics, the philosophy of mind, and the philosophy of language. Born in Vienna to a wealthy industrialist family of Jewish descent that had converted to Christianity, he initially trained as an aeronautical engineer before pursuing philosophy under Gottlob Frege and Bertrand Russell. Wittgenstein's early thought, crystallized in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), advanced a picture theory of language wherein propositions mirror atomic facts in the world, positing that meaningful discourse is confined to what can be logically depicted, with ethical and metaphysical matters falling outside language's boundsâ"Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." In a marked philosophical turn, his later work, notably the posthumously published Philosophical Investigations (1953), repudiated the Tractatus 's rigid logical atomism, arguing instead that meaning emerges from the practical use of language in diverse "language-games" embedded in shared forms of life, thereby dissolving traditional puzzles through attention to ordinary linguistic practices rather than idealized structures. This shift emphasized the contextual, rule-following nature of meaning and critiqued the possibility of a private language, influencing fields from linguistics to cognitive science. Wittgenstein's life reflected his intellectual intensity: he served as an artillery officer in the Austrian army during World War I, enduring capture at the Battle of Olmutz while refining the Tractatus in trenches and prison camps; later, he taught philosophy at Cambridge, holding the professorship from 1939 to 1947, yet intermittently withdrew to elementary school teaching in rural Austria, voluntary nursing in World War II, and architectural design for his sister's house. He inherited and largely donated his family's vast fortune, living ascetically amid personal torments including the suicides of three brothers and his own bouts of severe depression. Despite never authoring a systematic treatise beyond the Tractatus, his lectures, notes, and conversationsâcompiled by students like G.E.M. Anscombe ârevealed a method of philosophical therapy aimed at clarifying thought by exposing conceptual confusions.
